title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context from the previous pages: a spherical curve is described in polar coordinates (y = polar distance, x = longitude) with arc element dr and course angle ω. The governing relations are dy = dr·cos ω and dx·sin y = dr·sin ω. The first part was solved by the ansatz cos y = q cos r − p sin r, with tan r = dq/dp. Here r is at the same time the arc length (an angle) and a quantity fixed algebraically by p and q. This gives sin ω = √(1−p²−q²)/sin y, so dx = dr/√(1−p²−q²).

This page is the 'aliud tentamen' for the longitude. Euler splits x = ξ + φ. Dividing dξ = sin ω dr/sin y − dφ by sin²ξ, he sets sin ω/(sin y sin²ξ) = u/sin²r, with u 'free of r'. He then guesses the integral −cot ξ = −u cot r + t. Differentiating gives dφ = (du cot r − dt) sin²ξ, and cot ξ = (u cos r − t sin r)/sin r gives sin ξ and cos ξ.

Substituting sin²ξ into the ansatz gives sin ω(u² cos²r − 2tu sin r cos r + (1+t²) sin²r) = u sin y. Using sin ω = √W/sin y, with W = 1−p²−q², this becomes a quadratic form in (cos r, sin r) that must vanish identically:
(u²cos²r − 2tu sin r cos r + (1+t²) sin²r)·√W = u(1 + 2pq sin r cos r − p² sin²r − q² cos²r).
So r = 0 and r = 90° may be used:
- r = 0 gives u = (1−q²)/√W.
- r = 90° gives (1+t²)√W = u(1−p²), hence (1+t²)W = (1−p²)(1−q²), hence t² = p²q²/W.
- The sign t = −pq/√W is forced by the sin r cos r coefficient (Euler only says it must be taken).

He then differentiates u and t in p and q and forms du·cot r − dt with cot r = dp/dq. The point is that, after multiplying by sin²ξ, cot r must disappear. The next page completes this: dφ = p dq/((1−q²)√W), which agrees with the 'first solution' in Euler-angle variables (q = cos θ, p = −sin θ cos ψ).

The final recipe (next page):
1. Choose any algebraic relation between sin φ and q, and put s = dφ/dq.
2. Get p from √W = p/(s(1−q²)).
3. Then tan r = dq/dp, u and t as above, cos y = q cos r − p sin r, cot ξ = u cot r − t, and x = ξ + φ.

In effect this is an integral-free general solution: spherical curves whose arc length r is a circular angle with algebraic tangent, and whose coordinates are algebraic or circular. It is a spherical analogue of Euler's constructions of curves rectifiable by circular arcs.
errors: The displayed equation '(uu cos²r − 2tu sin r cos r + (1+tt) sin²r)(1 − pp − qq) = u sin²y' should have √(1−pp−qq), not (1−pp−qq). Euler's own subsequent specializations (uu√(1−pp−qq) = u(1−qq), etc.) use the square root, so this is a slip of pen or print.

In the first expression for du·cot r − dt the middle term is printed as −2q dp dq(1−pp−qq). The correct term is +2p²q dp dq: q(−1+2pp+qq) + q(1−qq) = 2ppq. Euler's second expression, '−q cot r(1−2pp−qq) + q cot r(1−qq)', does give 2ppq cot r and is correct.

In the last formula a factor p is pulled out but left inside as well. It should read du cot r − dt = p dq[(1−qq)cot²r + 2pq cot r + (1−pp)]/(1−pp−qq)^{3/2}. Only this form, multiplied by sin²ξ from the next page, gives dφ = p dq/((1−qq)√(1−pp−qq)), as Euler states.

Logical gap, acknowledged by Euler himself on the next page ('NB... desideratur criterium'): it is not shown a priori why cot r must cancel in dφ. Here it simply emerges from computation once dp = dq·cot r is used.
The sign choice t = −pq/√W is asserted ('sumi debet') rather than derived. It follows from matching the sin r cos r coefficient of the quadratic form.

ideas.what: Integrability ansatz −cot ξ = −u cot r + t, with u and t independent of r, used to integrate dξ/sin²ξ.
ideas.modern_name: Ansatz for an integral-free (Monge-type) parametrization of an underdetermined ODE system
ideas.usually_credited_to: Monge and Hilbert for the general theory of integral-free solutions; Euler for many concrete instances
ideas.where_published: Opera postuma 1862 (E819), from Adversaria T. I pp. 37–41; related spherical-curve rectification papers of Euler possibly exist (unsure)

ideas.what: An identity in r is treated as a quadratic form in (cos r, sin r) and its coefficients are found by specializing r = 0 and r = 90°.
ideas.modern_name: Coefficient matching / identical vanishing of a trigonometric quadratic form

ideas.what: General construction of spherical curves with algebraic coordinates whose arc length is a circular arc with algebraic tangent (tan r = dq/dp), with one arbitrary algebraic relation between sin φ and q.
ideas.modern_name: Spherical curves rectifiable by circular arcs; integral-free general solution
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (planar analogues: curves rectifiable by circular arcs / algebraic arcs)
ideas.where_published: Planar analogue in Euler's papers on rectifiable curves; the spherical version is perhaps only in these fragments (unsure)

missed.claim: Euler explicitly flags as missing an a priori criterion explaining why cot r drops out of dφ = (du cot r − dt) sin²ξ. The mechanism is that sin²ξ's denominator is proportional to the same quadratic (1−qq)cot²r + 2pq cot r + (1−pp) that appears in the numerator. This reflects the structure of the tangent-great-circle (dual) representation (p, q, √(1−p²−q²)) of the spherical curve. A conceptual explanation (e.g. via the polar/dual curve) is not given.
missed.quote: In superiori tentamine omnia manent usque ad valorem ipsius t, qui cum inventus sit ex aequatione quadratica, sumi debet t = −pq/√(1−pp−qq)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor. It is a small historical example of Euler groping toward integral-free solutions of underdetermined systems (Monge/Hilbert–Cartan). It is of interest to historians of the 'Monge problem' rather than to current research.

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra is a correct (up to typos) working-out of a concrete integral-free construction of spherical curves with circular rectification, consistent with Euler's known themes. It is interesting as a working note, but contains nothing a specialist would find startling.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image. Note that the '(1 − pp − qq)' factor in the key equation is in the printed original; it is an error of the source (should be √(1−pp−qq)), not of the transcription.
In the line 'du = ...' the image shows the numerator as 'pdp(1−qq) + qdq(−1+2pp+qq)', as transcribed; it is correct.
